si.how: Drafted card text and first-pass numbers from the Game Design Spec v2 and the cited sources

cards.title: Building the base
cards.text: Welcome to the Sea of Tranquility! The rover's blade can pile moon dirt, called regolith, over your habitat. Thick dirt blocks space radiation and keeps heat in.
cards.realBasis: NASA studies estimate 3–5 m of regolith shields a habitat, and packed regolith also insulates against heat swings.

cards.title: Noon heat
cards.text: The Sun is high and the ground outside is hotter than boiling water. The habitat is heating up.
cards.realBasis: Daytime temperatures near the lunar equator reach about 120 °C.

cards.title: Dust on the radiators
cards.text: Dark moon dust has settled on the cooling panels. Dust soaks up sunlight, so the panels can't cool the habitat well.

options.label: Brush them off during a moonwalk
Leave them (cooling works harder every Day)

specialist.label: Switch on the electrodynamic dust shield

cards.realBasis: On Apollo 16 and 17, dust on the rover's radiators overheated its batteries; NASA's dust shield cleared moon dust from radiator surfaces in 2025.

cards.title: Before sunset
cards.text: Night is coming, and it will last two weeks. Spend today's sunlight on science, or save it?

options.label: Keep that power in the batteries

specialist.label: Run the grow lights on spare sunlight

cards.realBasis: A lunar night lasts about 14 Earth days, which limits solar power on the Moon.

cards.title: Scout the lava-tube pit
cards.text: There's a deep pit nearby. It might lead to a cave, a natural shelter from solar storms.

options.label: Rappel to the edge for a close survey

cards.realBasis: Radar data suggests a pit in the Sea of Tranquility leads to a cave tens of metres long.

cards.title: Plant a pick-and-eat garden
cards.text: A small salad rack that grows in water, without soil, would give the crew fresh food.
cards.realBasis: The CSA says moon crops would grow without soil (hydroponics or aeroponics), favouring quick pick-and-eat crops.

cards.title: Long moonwalk to a crater
cards.text: A fresh crater 5 km away could hold rocks nobody has ever sampled.

specialist.label: Watch heart rates and pace the walk

cards.realBasis: Apollo flight surgeons used heart rates to judge effort during moonwalks; some early spacewalks were cut short by overheating.

cards.title: Cargo lander arrives
cards.text: A robot lander has touched down nearby with supplies from Earth.

options.label: Drive out for only the food crates

cards.realBasis: NASA buys robotic deliveries to the Moon from companies; planned deliveries include food, water, air and spare parts.

cards.title: Micrometeoroid strike
cards.text: Tiny bits of rock from a nearby impact have pitted one of your solar panels.

options.label: Live with it (less sunlight every Day)

cards.realBasis: NASA's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter found new craters forming faster than models predicted.

cards.title: Deep freeze
cards.text: Outside it's −130 °C, and the habitat walls are losing heat.

options.label: Heat only the sleeping module and bundle up

specialist.label: Take turns in the warm module while the doctor checks everyone

cards.realBasis: Nights near the lunar equator fall to about −130 °C.

cards.title: Frozen greenhouse water line
cards.text: A water pipe along the outer wall has iced up. The plants aren't getting water.

options.label: Warm the pipe with a heater cable
Fix it at sunrise (the plants go thirsty)

specialist.label: Hand-water the plants from the reserve tank

cards.realBasis: Without heat, the lunar night breaks hardware: India's Chandrayaan-3 lander and the U.S. Odysseus lander never woke up after theirs.

cards.title: Moonquake
cards.text: The ground shakes for more than 10 minutes. Did any seals crack?

specialist.label: Pressure-test the seals from the control panel

cards.realBasis: Apollo seismometers recorded shallow moonquakes up to magnitude 5.5 that shook for more than 10 minutes.

cards.title: Battery getting cold
cards.text: One battery pack sits in an unheated bay. Cold batteries hold less charge.

options.label: Move it into the warm module (it shares your heat)

cards.realBasis: Japan's SLIM lander survived lunar nights, but some of its battery cells began to fail afterward.

cards.title: Call with students on Earth
cards.text: Earth hangs in your night sky, so the radio link is easy. A school wants to talk to you!

options.label: Send a recording now and do a live Q&A at sunrise

cards.realBasis: A message from the Moon to Earth takes only seconds to arrive.

cards.title: Rover left outside
cards.text: The rover is parked in the open for the two-week night.

options.label: Let it freeze and hope it restarts

cards.realBasis: Most landers without a heat source haven't survived the lunar night.

cards.title: Mold in the greenhouse
cards.text: Damp leaves have started to grow mold.

options.label: Dry them out with the fans on high

specialist.label: Cut away the dead leaves, then wipe and dry the plants

cards.realBasis: Mold grew on the ISS zinnias in 2015 after too much water; Scott Kelly cleaned and dried them and saved two of the four.

cards.title: Can't sleep in the long dark
cards.text: Two weeks without a sunrise is scrambling the crew's body clocks.

options.label: Give the crew a rest day

specialist.label: Set the cabin lights to a day–night colour cycle

cards.realBasis: The ISS switched to LED lights that can shift colour to help astronauts stay alert or get sleepy.

cards.title: Two weeks of dark sky
cards.text: With no air and a slow-turning Moon, a telescope can stare at one target for days.

options.label: Set up the telescope outside and track one galaxy all night
Photograph the sky from a window (the cover lets heat out)

cards.realBasis: China's Chang'E 3 lander ran an ultraviolet telescope on the Moon; with no air and slow rotation it could watch one target for long stretches.
